opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting shifts happening right now. For a long time the mental model for inference was a chatbot: a user sends a prompt, maybe a few hundred or a few thousand tokens, and you generate a response. Chips and systems were designed around that, either big batched prefill or relatively short decoding.

Coding and agent workloads look quite different. First, the contexts are much longer. An agent working in a codebase might carry tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens: files, tool outputs, the history of what it's tried. That puts enormous pressure on memory capacity and memory bandwidth, because the KV cache grows with context length, and during decoding you're mostly bottlenecked on reading that cache and the weights, not on raw FLOPs. So the balance between compute and memory, which hardware designers have to fix years in advance, gets pushed further toward memory.

Second, agents generate a lot of tokens, and latency matters in a new way. If a model is going to take fifty steps, calling tools, reading results, thinking, then writing code, the per-token latency compounds. A human chatting can tolerate some delay; an agent loop that's ten times slower per step is ten times slower end to end. So you care about both throughput, to keep costs down, and low-latency decoding, and those pull in somewhat different directions on chip design.

Third, the workload becomes much more irregular. You have prefix sharing, because many requests start from the same system prompt or the same repository, so caching and reusing KV states becomes important. You have branching, where you sample multiple attempts and verify them. You have interleaving with tool execution, so the accelerator might sit idle waiting for a test suite to run unless the scheduler is smart. That's as much a systems and software problem as a silicon problem.

And that's part of why I think architecture and hardware co-design matters a lot. If the attention mechanism's cost grows with context, people will explore things like state-space models, hybrid architectures, or more compressed attention variants that reduce memory traffic. Hardware people then have to guess: are workloads going to be dominated by attention over long contexts, or by these more recurrent-style layers? Making that bet years out is really hard.

So my short answer is: agentic workloads make inference more memory-bound, more latency-sensitive, and more dynamic. The chips that win will likely be the ones with a lot of fast memory and flexible enough software stacks to handle these messier patterns, not just the ones with the highest peak FLOPs on paper.

r001.rationale: The response identifies tool execution as part of agent workloads, describing agents calling tools and interleaving model work with tool execution.

r002.rationale: It discusses tool-related idle time and scheduling, but does not state that a narrow focus on model execution speed can neglect host connectivity needed for tool use.

r003.rationale: It describes possible changes to attention and model architectures, but does not communicate that high-level AI architecture is relatively stable while substantial changes continue beneath it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the workload really has shifted underneath the hardware. Two or three years ago, if you were designing a chip or a serving system, you were mostly optimizing for a chatbot: a person types a question, the model generates a few hundred tokens, and the main thing you cared about was prefill throughput and maybe time to first token. Agents and coding workloads look very different.

The first big change is the ratio of decode to prefill. An agent is generating a lot of tokens, it's calling tools, reading the results, generating more, and it's doing this in long loops. So the workload becomes much more decode-heavy, and decode is fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. You're streaming the weights and the KV cache through the chip for every single token. That pushes the design toward more HBM bandwidth, more on-chip memory, and better ways to batch across many concurrent agents so you can actually use the FLOPs you paid for.

The second change is context length. Coding agents want to see an entire repository, the test output, the history of what they've tried. So the KV cache gets huge, and now the question is where it lives and how you move it around. A lot of the interesting work, things like paged attention, prefix caching, KV cache offloading to CPU memory or across nodes, is really about managing that state. I'd argue the memory hierarchy, not peak FLOPs, is where the hardware competition is now.

The third thing, which people underrate, is that agents are not latency-sensitive in the same way a chat is. If a coding agent is going to run for ten minutes, you don't need every token in 20 milliseconds. That opens up a lot of room for throughput-oriented designs, for speculative decoding, for larger batches, for cheaper hardware per token. And the economics matter because these agents burn through tokens at a rate no human would. So I think we'll see chips and systems that are much more specialized for high-throughput, long-context decode, and a lot of the software work, things like FlashAttention and its successors, is about getting the most out of whatever that hardware turns out to be.

r001.rationale: It describes agents calling tools, reading their results, and generating more tokens, making external tool use part of the workload.

r002.rationale: It discusses memory bandwidth, throughput, and token cost, but does not say that focusing on model execution speed can neglect host connectivity for tool use.

r003.rationale: It describes changes in workloads and hardware needs, but does not state that high-level AI architecture has stayed relatively stable while lower-level systems continue to change.

astra-6.text:
I think they make it much harder to know what workload you're designing for. With coding agents, you might have a model reading a large codebase, generating some code, calling a tool, waiting for a test to finish, and then coming back to the model. So it's a loop, and the bottleneck can move between those stages.

Even within the model, processing a long prompt and generating tokens one at a time have different hardware requirements. You care about compute, memory bandwidth, and the capacity to keep context around. And if the next step depends on the previous result, latency matters a lot. High throughput alone doesn't necessarily make that agent finish its task faster.

That creates a tension because chip design takes years, while these workloads can change quite quickly. You want specialization for efficiency, but you also want enough flexibility to support changes in the model architecture and how inference is run. To me, that makes designing the hardware and software together especially important. The metric you ultimately care about is how quickly and cheaply the system completes a useful task, and that isn't captured by peak FLOPS alone.

r001.rationale: It describes an agent loop that includes calling a tool and waiting for a test, beyond model execution alone.

r002.rationale: It contrasts throughput with task completion speed, but does not say that narrow focus on model speed neglects host connectivity for tool use.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing workloads, models, and inference, but does not distinguish stable high-level AI architecture from substantial changes beneath it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they make the hardware design problem a lot more of a moving target. When you design a chip, you’re making bets about what workloads will look like several years out. And with coding agents, even the shape of inference is changing pretty quickly.

An agent might read a large codebase, generate a little bit of code, call a tool, wait for the result, and then do another round. So you have this mixture of processing long contexts and generating tokens, with tool calls in between. Those phases stress the hardware differently. Processing the context tends to benefit from a lot of compute, while generating tokens can be much more constrained by memory bandwidth and moving data around.

And then there’s the question of how much work you do in parallel. Are you running one agent, or are you trying a hundred possible solutions and testing them? That changes the balance between latency and throughput. You might care less about how fast one token comes out and more about how quickly you get a working solution.

So I’d be cautious about optimizing a chip too narrowly for today’s workload. You still want efficient matrix multiplication, but memory capacity, bandwidth, communication, and the ability to support different execution patterns become really important. The interesting challenge is figuring out which properties will stay stable as the models and the agent systems keep changing.

r001.rationale: It describes agents calling a tool, waiting for its result, and continuing, distinguishing the workload from model execution alone.

r002.rationale: It warns against narrow chip optimization and mentions communication, but does not identify host connectivity needed for tool use.

r003.rationale: It says models and agent systems keep changing and asks which properties will stay stable, but does not state that high-level AI architecture is relatively stable while lower-level details change.
